transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 13:00 PST | Duration: 45 mins | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Sarah Patel (Argentum), Tom Briggs (Argentum), Leah Morgan (Argentum)

Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect): Discussed Dedicated capacity needs, isolation/VPC options, burst vs reserved strategy, autoscaling expectations, security compliance (SOC2/KMS), benchmarking plan and next steps to share pricing and run pilot.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intros, um, I'm Maya, I'm the account executive on the Redwood team. Diego from our solutions engineering is here for the deep infra stuff.
00:12 Speaker 2 (Diego): Hi hi, thanks. Hey Sarah, Tom, Leah, nice to meet you.
00:17 Speaker 3 (Sarah): Hey, thanks for doing this. We're excited — we've been evaluating a few options and wanted to dig into what Dedicated buys us over Hosted and what the Private path looks like.
00:28 Speaker 1 (Maya): Totally. High level — Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, consistent throughput, and isolation from multi-tenant noisy neighbors; Private is the on-prem/VPC option if you need customer-controlled networking. Today we want to understand your workload to recommend sizing, burst strategy, and any compliance constraints.
00:46 Speaker 3 (Sarah): Great. Quick background: Argentum does real-time risk scoring and doc extraction for mortgage originations. Latency matters — we target p95 under 400ms for small prompt flows, but some batch jobs are okay with minutes. We generate embeddings for search nightly.
01:05 Speaker 4 (Tom): We run a Kubernetes-based infra on AWS, a mix of T4 and A10-ish for training; for inference we haven't standardized. We're worried about token cost and also keeping results on-prem or encrypted — regulator asks around data residency.
01:21 Speaker 2 (Diego): Okay, so two profiles: latency-critical online calls, and large offline embedding batches. For Dedicated we'd typically recommend a pool of GPUs sized for your p95 and throughput targets, plus a burst plan for peak times. Can you share typical QPS and payload sizes?
01:37 Speaker 3 (Sarah): Right now peak is about 70 QPS across a few endpoints, average payload is 350 tokens per request, but we have spikes up to 300 QPS during batch windows that kick off concurrently.
01:50 Speaker 2 (Diego): Got it. So 70 steady, spikes to 300 occasionally. For that profile, a Dedicated cluster with reserved instances sized for 100 QPS steady plus burst capacity that can autoscale to handle spikes would make sense. Our Dedicated offering supports reserved GPU pools and a burst policy to spill into either held spare capacity or private burst on our hosted fleet depending on policy.
02:12 Speaker 4 (Tom): Wait, spill into hosted fleet — that has implications for data isolation. We need to keep PII inside our VPC. How does the burst work without sending data off-prem?
02:24 Speaker 2 (Diego): Good call. We have two burst modes: 1) within Dedicated—if you have idle capacity in your reserved pool we can burst there; 2) cross-pool burst to Redwood's hosted nodes which is faster but not acceptable if you require all compute inside your VPC. For strict isolation you can configure a Private deployment or enable on-prem bursts if we provision extra reserved capacity. There's also encrypted transit and optional SAML-backed access.
02:46 Speaker 5 (Leah): So for compliance we likely need VPC-only compute. We are SOC2 in process and need audit logs/KMS integration and customer-managed keys.
02:55 Speaker 2 (Diego): We support KMS/HSM integrations and customer-managed keys for Private. For Dedicated we offer KMS options and granular audit logs; the difference is whether the compute plane is in your VPC. If you need VPC-only compute, that's the Private deployment. Dedicated can be isolated to a customer-only pool but still in Redwood-managed infra — that meets many enterprise controls but may not satisfy air-gapped requirements.
03:18 Speaker 3 (Sarah): Can you explain isolation more — like is Dedicated single-tenant GPU nodes, or shared nodes with tenant-aware scheduling?
03:25 Speaker 2 (Diego): Dedicated is single-tenant at the pool level. Your workloads run on GPUs reserved for your account; we don't colocate other customers' workloads on those GPUs. We do share the orchestration plane unless you opt for Private. There can be multi-tenancy at the control plane layer, but the compute is isolated.
03:41 Speaker 4 (Tom): Cool. What about autoscaling speed — we can't tolerate long spin-up times during a sudden surge.
03:47 Speaker 2 (Diego): We have fast warm pools and cold scaling. Warm pools keep a fraction of capacity hot to cut cold-starts; you can set scale policies with target p95 and max burst. Cold GPU provisioning can take minutes, warm pools are typically seconds to route traffic. For guaranteed fast burst you can commit to a specific burst capacity in the contract.
04:04 Speaker 3 (Sarah): What's the typical latency penalty for large context windows — we sometimes pass 2k-4k tokens for document summarization.
04:11 Speaker 2 (Diego): It depends on model and quantization; our runtimes are optimized for attention and KV cache. For 2k tokens p95 will rise but we've tuned kernels for longer context. Diego: We should run an end-to-end bench with your 2k samples.
04:26 Speaker 2 (Diego): (Diego) Yeah, let's do that. We'll need sample prompts and some target SLAs. We often recommend quantized variants for cost trade-offs; quantization can reduce memory and cost but may impact quality slightly for some tasks.
04:38 Speaker 5 (Leah): On security — we need SSO (SAML), role-based access, detailed audit logs, and retention settings for logs. Do you expose per-token cost breakdowns? Compliance needs proof of cost and usage for audits.
04:52 Speaker 1 (Maya): Yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns and per-route dashboards; RBAC and SAML are supported, you can get audit exports. We'll send the security whitepaper after this.
05:02 Speaker 3 (Sarah): Also, how do you handle model updates? We need pinned versions and a canary rollout to ensure no regressions in risk scoring thresholds.
05:11 Speaker 2 (Diego): We support model pinning and rollout policies — canary, A/B, automatic fallback to pinned model variants. You can also tie evaluations to regression alerts. We'll demo that in the pilot.
05:21 Speaker 4 (Tom): Pricing question — what's the economics between hosted, Dedicated, and Private? If we reserve 10 GPUs vs pay-as-you-go hosted what's the break-even?
05:32 Speaker 1 (Maya): Pricing depends on commit term and GPU type. Dedicated has a lower per-token cost because of reserved capacity; Private has additional platform fees. We'll send a tailored TCO we can run with your QPS and token volumes. Typical break-even often happens within a few months for steady high-volume workloads.
05:47 Speaker 3 (Sarah): For our batch embeddings job — can Dedicated run offline batch jobs without impacting latency-critical endpoints?
05:54 Speaker 2 (Diego): Yes, you can configure scheduling and priority. We support workload tiers so batch jobs are lower priority and won't steal capacity from latency endpoints. Also caching helps for prefix reuse across calls.
06:06 Speaker 5 (Leah): Any constraints on model types? We use some fine-tuned open models and also evaluate closed models.
06:13 Speaker 2 (Diego): We support a catalog of open models, private model hosting, and you can bring your own models. There are kernel selection and quantization considerations per model; for fine-tuned models we typically recommend benchmarking to pick optimized kernels.
06:25 Speaker 3 (Sarah): Okay, what would a pilot look like?
06:28 Speaker 1 (Maya): Pilot usually includes: reserved pilot capacity for X GPUs for 2-4 weeks, benchmark run with your sample traffic, integration of SSO/KMS as needed, and success criteria defined — e.g., p95 < 400ms for online flows, cost per 1k tokens below a threshold, and no PII leaving VPC (if Private).
06:46 Speaker 4 (Tom): Timeline? We want to decide by end of month. Can you support a pilot starting next week?
06:52 Speaker 1 (Maya): We can aim for a pilot start in 7–10 days pending contract/NDAs and engineering kickoff. Diego will outline the benchmark plan today.
06:59 Speaker 2 (Diego): Bench plan: we need a representative sample set — 50k online requests and 10k long-context summarization requests, plus 5M tokens of embeddings for nightly batch. We'll run runs on a quantized and base model variant and produce latency and token-cost reports.
07:18 Speaker 5 (Leah): For ingress — what's the easiest way to push sample data? S3?
07:22 Speaker 2 (Diego): S3 with presigned URLs is easiest; we can also support secure upload into a private bucket if you're doing Private. We'll share a template.
07:30 Speaker 3 (Sarah): Any gotchas around KV cache warm-up affecting latency numbers?
07:34 Speaker 2 (Diego): Yes, initial cold requests will be slower. We'll instruct to run warmup traffic to prime caches; our benchmark will include cold and warm trials. Also continuous batching and prefix caching can improve effective throughput.
07:47 Speaker 4 (Tom): How do you handle model fallbacks when a newer model underperforms? We've seen production drift cause bad outcomes.
07:53 Speaker 2 (Diego): We have automated rollbacks and canary thresholds tied to eval sets and production metrics. If quality drops, traffic automatically shifts back to previous model. We can also run shadow testing.
08:05 Speaker 1 (Maya): A few clarifying Qs on procurement: Who owns procurement paperwork and who will sign NDAs?
08:11 Speaker 3 (Sarah): Procurement is me and Tom; legal will be pulled in. We'll likely want customer-specific data processing addendum and SOC2 report before purchase.
08:19 Speaker 5 (Leah): Also SLA requirements — uptime and latency SLOs matter; for Dedicated we expect better guarantees.
08:24 Speaker 1 (Maya): Yes, Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; specific terms are in the enterprise contract. We'll include a redline-friendly draft with pricing.
08:33 Speaker 4 (Tom): Technical: Do you allow us to bring our own KMS keys for encryption at rest?
08:38 Speaker 2 (Diego): Yes, we support customer-managed keys for both Dedicated and Private. For Dedicated there are integrations; for full on-prem keys and hardware HSM we recommend Private.
08:49 Speaker 3 (Sarah): Any monitoring hooks? We want tracing to our existing observability stack.
08:54 Speaker 2 (Diego): We offer tracing hooks and export integrations; token-level cost telemetry is accessible and you can pull traces into your Sentry/NewRelic or internal tracing. We'll map the endpoints for you.
09:05 Speaker 1 (Maya): Alright, seems like we're aligned on pilot scope. Diego, to confirm — you'll share the benchmark template and suggested GPU sizing?
09:12 Speaker 2 (Diego): Yep, I'll send a sizing recommendation based on 70 steady QPS, 300 spike, and the sample context lengths. Expect a suggested configuration: 4 x A10-ish reserved GPUs for steady with 2 warm GPUs for burst and optional 4 GPU cold burst pool depending on contract. We'll include quantized variants too.
09:29 Speaker 5 (Leah): That configuration aligns with our initial thinking. If we go VPC-only, cost will be higher but compliance is non-negotiable.
09:37 Speaker 3 (Sarah): OK. Can you also include an estimate for monthly cost and per-million-token cost for each scenario (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)?
09:44 Speaker 1 (Maya): Yes, we'll include a TCO worksheet and break-even analysis.
09:49 Speaker 4 (Tom): Next steps recap?
09:52 Speaker 1 (Maya): I can run that — 1) Maya to send pricing, SLA, and security whitepaper; 2) Diego to share benchmark plan, sizing, and sample upload instructions; 3) Leah to share compliance stakeholders and log requirements; 4) Sarah/Tom to confirm decision timeline and pilot start date.
10:12 Speaker 3 (Sarah): Sounds good. We aim to decide by 2026-03-25.
10:16 Speaker 1 (Maya): Great — we'll follow up via email with the docs and a proposed calendar invite for the engineering kickoff. Thanks everyone.
10:23 Speaker 2 (Diego): Thanks all.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mislabels, some proper nouns transcribed imperfectly (A10-ish may be transcribed as A10-Ish), and small filler words included.

End of transcript.
